the M epitope is a trisaccha-ride and the A epitope is a tetrasacchar-ide.

the A and M epitope specific mAbs recognize distinct oligosaccharide epitopes of the Brucella O-polysacchride, and the fine specificity of these mAbs is revealed by the synthesis of unique oligosaccharidic antigens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fine specificity of the A and M monocional antibodies, and the development of a new synthetic glycoconjugate vaccine for Brucella abortus.
the fine structure of the A and M epitope and the development of a new class of diagnostic reagents.
the structural characterization of the epitopes that define the A and M epitope specificity and the structural basis of their recognition by mAbs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fine specificity of the A and M monocloal antibodies is dictated by the length and the sequence of the Rha4NFoligomer.
the fine specificity of the A and M mAbs is determined by the number of Rha4NFos in the epitopes and the nature of the linkage between them.
the A and M epitope structures are defined by the α1,2 linkage and the terminal Rha residue, respectively.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a combination of chemical synthesis and monoclonal antibodies has allowed us to define the structural basis of Brucella serological specificity.
the A and M epitope mAbs are all of the groove type, and the A epitopes are more extended than the M epitopes.
the A and M epitope specific mAbs bind to a common epitope, a trisacchride, and that the A epitope specific mAb binds to a longer epitope.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the fine specificity of mAbs can be determined using synthetic glycoconjugate antigens and that the binding sites of mAbs are sufficiently large to accommodate the polymeric nature of the O-polysaccaride antigen.
the fine specificity of the A and M monoclassical antibodies is dictated by a combination of the length of the polymeric sequence and the number and type of α-linked Rha4NF residues in the epitope.
the binding sites for A and M specific antibodies are sufficiently different to allow for the discrimination of these two closely related epitopes.
